opus-5.5.text:
I usually look at it from a few angles rather than just counting GPUs.

The first thing I ask is: what's the ratio of compute to researchers? A team can have a lot of cards in absolute terms, but if you have a hundred people sharing them, each person is effectively queuing for days to run one meaningful experiment. What really matters is whether an individual researcher can test an idea, see the result, and iterate within a reasonable loop — ideally a day or two for the core experiments. If the iteration cycle stretches into weeks, the team is compute-constrained no matter what the headline number says.

The second is whether the team can afford to fail. Good research needs a lot of experiments that don't work. If every run has to be justified in advance because it's so expensive, people become conservative, they only try the safe ideas, and you lose the exploratory part that actually produces breakthroughs. So one signal I watch is: are people running small-scale ablations freely, or is every experiment a negotiation?

Third, can they do the experiments at the scale where the interesting phenomena show up? Some behaviors only emerge at larger scale, so if you can only validate ideas on small models, you may draw the wrong conclusions. A team with enough compute can run a scaling ladder — small, medium, larger — and check whether a trend holds before betting big.

And finally, it's about how compute is allocated, not just how much there is. I've seen teams with plenty of resources still feel starved because allocation is fragmented, or the infrastructure is unreliable, so a lot of compute is wasted on failed jobs and debugging. Utilization and infra quality are part of the answer.

So roughly: if researchers can iterate fast, fail cheaply, and verify ideas at a meaningful scale, I'd say they have enough. If any of those three breaks, they don't — even if the number of GPUs sounds impressive.

r001.rationale: The response describes practical signs of sufficient compute, such as fast iteration and meaningful-scale experiments. It does not state that compute is never enough for an enthusiastic research team.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and honestly the answer is less about the raw number than people think.

The first thing I look at is the ratio of compute to people. Not the total GPU count. A team of fifteen with two thousand GPUs is in a very different position from a team of two hundred with eight thousand. What matters is how many experiments each researcher can run in parallel without waiting in a queue. If your people are spending half their time fighting for allocation, you're compute-starved regardless of what your cluster looks like on paper.

The second thing I look at is whether the team can afford to be wrong. Research is mostly failure. If every large run has to succeed because you only get one shot a quarter, people stop taking risks. They run the safe experiment, the incremental one. You can see it in the culture almost immediately. Teams with enough compute have a certain looseness, a willingness to burn a week on something that probably won't work. Teams without it get conservative, and conservative research doesn't produce frontier results.

Third, I ask about the gap between the biggest thing they've trained and the biggest thing they want to train. If that gap is more than an order of magnitude, they're not really in the game they think they're in. They're doing small-scale proxies and hoping the conclusions transfer, and often they don't.

And then there's a softer signal. I ask researchers what they'd do with ten times more compute. If they have a specific answer immediately, they've been thinking about it because they feel the constraint every day. If they have to think about it, they're probably fine. Hunger shows up fast when you ask that question.

One caveat though. Enough compute is a moving target. What counted as enough two years ago is a rounding error now. So I don't think any team ever has enough in an absolute sense. The question is whether they have enough relative to the questions they're actually trying to answer, and whether their access is growing at least as fast as the field is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says no team has enough compute in an absolute sense because the target keeps moving, but it does not state that compute is never enough specifically for research team members who are enthusiastic about working.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at whether compute is constraining the team’s ability to learn. Can they test their main hypotheses, run the necessary controls, and follow up on surprising results? Or are they constantly postponing useful experiments because the queue is too long?

Having enough compute doesn’t mean everyone can run anything they want. You still need priorities. But if researchers routinely spend more time waiting for experiments than designing and interpreting them, that’s a sign they may need more.

I’d also ask: if you doubled their compute tomorrow, what would they do with it? If they can name specific experiments and explain what decisions those experiments would inform, that’s a much stronger case than simply saying they want to train a bigger model.

r001.rationale: The response says a team may need more compute when waits routinely displace research work, but it does not state that compute is never enough for enthusiastic team members.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d judge it by the team’s iteration speed. Can researchers test their main ideas, get results, and use those results to decide what to try next? If promising experiments are constantly waiting for GPUs, compute is probably a bottleneck. If GPUs are sitting idle because the team is still figuring out what to run, more compute won’t necessarily help.

So “enough” depends on the research agenda. I’d look at whether the team can run its essential experiments, reproduce results, and explore a few alternatives without every run becoming a major resource decision.

r001.rationale: The response says enough compute depends on the research agenda and whether experiments are blocked; it does not state that compute is never enough for an enthusiastic team.
